newsReadings.passage:
The year 2026 will be one of the four warmest years since records began, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), published as the COP31 climate summit opened in Antalya, Türkiye. The figures make stark reading. The global average surface temperature for January to September 2026 stood about 1.47 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial average, and the past twelve years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years ranking as the top four. "El Niño and indeed the state of the global climate in 2026 gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts," said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo.

Much of the additional heat is being driven by a very strong El Niño event, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December. El Niño does not create new heat; rather, it releases heat that has been stored in the ocean, and the ocean in 2026 is the warmest ever measured. "We are supercharging our weather, and El Niño will be a risk multiplier," Saulo warned. "Heatwaves, tropical cyclones and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for." The event is expected to keep unleashing extreme weather well into 2027, long after the current year has ended.

The oceans lie at the heart of the story. They absorb around 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and Earth's energy imbalance — the gap between incoming solar energy and outgoing heat — has reached its highest level since monitoring began. As a result, 2026 is on track to become the tenth successive year of record ocean warmth, sea level stands at the highest level ever recorded, and sea-surface temperatures set monthly records through the year. The warming ocean, in turn, supplies more energy and moisture to storms, making them more destructive when they reach land.

On land, the retreat of the world's ice continues. The mass of ice lost from glaciers in 2025 alone would have filled five Olympic swimming pools every second of the year, and freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014. The dangers are not abstract. In Nepal this year, the collapse of ice and rock in high mountains triggered flash floods, a vivid example of the compound risks facing communities in fragile, warming terrain, where one hazard can rapidly cascade into another.

That figure points to a second, quieter crisis: water. As glaciers shrink and rainfall patterns shift, the water stored in snow, ice and underground reserves — the supply on which farms and cities depend in dry seasons — has been falling steadily since 2014. For communities already living close to the margin, the loss of that natural reservoir means deeper droughts, smaller harvests and harder choices about where scarce water should go, turning a geophysical trend into a daily question of livelihood.

The human cost is already immense. Hundreds of millions of people have been exposed to unbearable extreme heat this year, while the economic damage from extreme weather has mounted across every continent. The WMO report, compiled from data available up to September, is intended as an authoritative, science-based baseline for the COP31 negotiations — the evidence against which promises made in Antalya will ultimately be judged.

The report's central message is that the climate system is now moving beyond the range of past experience. The 1.5-degree threshold that the Paris Agreement sought to defend is being overshot, and the question facing governments is no longer whether warming is happening, but how much further it will go — and whether the measures taken in the coming years can slow a transformation that, on the evidence of 2026, is accelerating. Whether the summit's eventual successor, COP32 in Addis Ababa in 2027, can turn that evidence into agreement remains the decisive question of the decade.

newsReadings.passage:
The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorised Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites designed to operate as data centres in space, in what the agency described as the first authorisation in American history for a constellation of orbital data centres. The network, known as Starmind, would process vast amounts of information in orbit for use on Earth, driven by the rapidly growing demand for computing power from artificial intelligence. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr called the decision a historic first in the race for AI, and the approval gives SpaceX until 2040 to put the full constellation in place.

The scale of the plan is difficult to grasp. SpaceX first sought permission in an application filed on 30 January 2026, proposing up to a million orbital compute modules operating at altitudes of between 500 and 2,000 kilometres and linked by high-bandwidth laser connections. The company describes Starmind as capturing solar energy in space to power low-cost, high-performance AI computing for Earth, and its application even presents the project as a first step towards becoming what physicists call a Kardashev II-level civilisation — one able to harness the full power of its star. SpaceX has said it plans to launch its first orbital data centres in 2027, with broader deployment beginning as early as 2028.

That ambition dwarfs everything currently in orbit. SpaceX already operates just over 11,000 of its Starlink broadband satellites, the largest constellation ever assembled, yet Starmind would increase the total number of satellites around Earth roughly fifty-fold. Even without it, the number of active satellites is projected to rise from about 15,000 today to a further 58,000 by 2030. Under the terms of its licence, SpaceX must deploy its first Starmind satellite by November 2033, a tenth of the constellation — 100,000 satellites — by November 2035, and half by November 2038. Building and launching at that pace will depend on Starship, the company's giant new rocket, becoming fully operational.

The case for putting data centres in space rests on two scarce resources on Earth: energy and water. A conventional data centre consumes enormous amounts of electricity and, in many designs, water for cooling. In orbit, by contrast, solar power is uninterrupted and the cold of space offers natural cooling. That logic has attracted rivals as well as SpaceX: Google and Blue Origin are pursuing similar concepts, and the FCC's decision may prove to be the starting gun for a wider competition to industrialise low Earth orbit.

Yet the decision has also alarmed many scientists. Critics warn of a steep rise in the risk of collisions and orbital debris, of damage to astronomy from a sky crowded with bright satellites, and of the environmental consequences of manufacturing and launching a million spacecraft. Earthjustice, an environmental law organisation, noted that the approval was granted without an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC, for its part, maintained that Starmind operates consistently with its orbital debris rules, and it refused one part of SpaceX's request: satellites operating above 600 kilometres will not be allowed to retire into so-called graveyard orbits, but must instead be brought down to burn up in the atmosphere.

Even SpaceX has cautioned that the technology remains unproven. In a filing ahead of its planned public listing, the company warned that orbital data centres rely on technologies that have not yet been demonstrated at scale and may never achieve commercial viability. The licence, then, is best understood not as a guarantee but as a deadline-driven test: fourteen years to turn a vision of computing powered by sunlight above the atmosphere into a working system — or to discover, at great expense, that some frontiers are better left unexplored.
